claim: Alternative pre-mRNA splicing (AS) significantly diversifies the neuronal proteome.
source: Although alternative pre-mRNA splicing (AS) significantly diversifies the neuronal proteome, the extent of AS is still unknown due in part to the large number of diverse cell types in the brain.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific understanding about the role of AS in neurons.

claim: The extent of AS is still unknown due in part to the large number of diverse cell types in the brain.
source: Although alternative pre-mRNA splicing (AS) significantly diversifies the neuronal proteome, the extent of AS is still unknown due in part to the large number of diverse cell types in the brain.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a limitation in current knowledge based on the complexity of brain tissue.

claim: The Junction Usage Model (JUM) allows the comprehensive profiling of both known and novel AS events from specific RNA-seq libraries.
source: The method, the Junction Usage Model (JUM), allows the comprehensive profiling of both known and novel AS events from specific RNA-seq libraries.
evidence: This describes the capability of the JUM method used in the study.

claim: Many diverse and novel pre-mRNA isoforms are preferentially expressed in one class of clock neuron and also absent from the more standard Drosophila head RNA preparation.
source: The results show that many diverse and novel pre-mRNA isoforms are preferentially expressed in one class of clock neuron and also absent from the more standard Drosophila head RNA preparation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of neuron-specific RNA-seq data.

claim: AS events are enriched in potassium channels important for neuronal firing.
source: These AS events are enriched in potassium channels important for neuronal firing, and there are also cycling isoforms with no detectable underlying transcriptional oscillations.
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis of the AS events identified in the study.

claim: There are cycling isoforms with no detectable underlying transcriptional oscillations.
source: These AS events are enriched in potassium channels important for neuronal firing, and there are also cycling isoforms with no detectable underlying transcriptional oscillations.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-course analysis of AS patterns in the study.

claim: Massive AS regulation in the brain is likely important for circadian regulation.
source: The results suggest massive AS regulation in the brain that is also likely important for circadian regulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings regarding the role of AS in circadian neurons.

claim: Organisms ranging from cyanobacteria to mammals contain circadian clocks that synchronize physiology and behavior to time-of-day environmental cues, such as light and temperature.
source: Organisms ranging from cyanobacteria to mammals contain circadian clocks that synchronize physiology and behavior to time-of-day environmental cues, such as light and temperature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clocks across organisms.

claim: Drosophila exhibits robust circadian clocks that control a diverse range of behaviors such as activity, sleep, mating and feeding.
source: The fruit fly, Drosophila, is no exception and exhibits robust circadian clocks that control a diverse range of behaviors such as activity, sleep, mating and feeding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila circadian biology.

claim: The core molecular machinery of the circadian clock is a set of transcription factors that act together to drive cycling or time-of-day dependent transcription of at least 20% of genes in the genome.
source: The core molecular machinery of the circadian clock is a set of transcription factors that act together to drive cycling or time-of-day dependent transcription of at least 20% of genes in the genome (Abruzzi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The heterodimeric transcription factor CLOCK/CYCLE (CLK/CYC) binds to the promoters of many direct target genes and activates their transcription late in the day.
source: The heterodimeric transcription factor CLOCK/CYCLE (CLK/CYC) binds to the promoters of many direct target genes and activates their transcription late in the day.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: Timeless (Tim) and Period (Per) encode transcriptional repressors that re-enter the nucleus in the late night and act as part of a negative feedback loop to turn off CLK/CYC transcription.
source: Two of these direct target genes, Timeless (Tim) and Period (Per), encode transcriptional repressors that re-enter the nucleus in the late night and act as part of a negative feedback loop to turn off CLK/CYC transcription (Edery et al., 1994; Naidoo et al., 1999; Sehgal et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Cryptochrome (CRY) and the kinase Doubletime (Dbt) contribute to the degradation of Tim/Per in the early morning.
source: In the early morning, the photoreceptor, Cryptochrome (CRY) and the kinase, Doubletime (Dbt) contribute to the degradation of Tim/Per (Kim et al., 2007; Kloss et al., 1998; Emery et al., 1998; Stanewsky et al., 1998; Ceriani et al., 1999; Hunter-Ensor et al., 1996; Syed et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The Drosophila brain molecular clock resides in a neural network of ~150 neurons.
source: In the Drosophila brain, this molecular clock resides in a neural network of ~150 neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila circadian system.

claim: Circadian neurons are divided into seven subgroups including three groups of dorsal neurons (DNs; DN1, DN2, and DN3), three groups of lateral neurons (ventral and dorsal lateral neurons; large and small LNvs and LNds, respectively) and the lateral posterior neurons (LPNs) with discrete behavior functions.
source: These neurons are divided into seven subgroups including three groups of dorsal neurons (DNs; DN1, DN2, and DN3), three groups of lateral neurons (ventral and dorsal lateral neurons; large and small LNvs and LNds, respectively) and the lateral posterior neurons (LPNs) with discrete behavior functions; reviewed in (Peschel and Helfrich-Förster, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Circadian neurons make up a small portion of the Drosophila brain (~0.1%) and head (~0.05%).
source: These neurons make up a small portion of the Drosophila brain (~0.1%) and head (~0.05%).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the proportion of circadian neurons in Drosophila tissues.

claim: It is difficult to profile specialized circadian neurons as part of studies that focus on Drosophila brain and head tissues.
source: As a result, it is difficult to profile these specialized neurons as part of studies that focus on Drosophila brain and head tissues (Hughes et al., 2012; Rodriguez et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and reflects a methodological challenge.

claim: Three subgroups (DN1s, LNds, and LNvs) of circadian neurons as well as one non-circadian outgroup (Dopaminergic or tyrosine-hydroxylase (TH) expressing neurons) were labeled with GFP using neuron-specific drivers and manually isolated.
source: To learn more about the function of these neurons within the circadian neuronal circuit, three subgroups (DN1s, LNds, and LNvs) of these neurons as well as one non-circadian outgroup (Dopaminergic or tyrosine-hydroxylase (TH) expressing neurons) were labeled with GFP using neuron-specific drivers and manually isolated (Abruzzi et al., 2015; Abruzzi et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in previous studies that generated the data analyzed here.

claim: Illumina RNA-seq datasets from these neurons were analyzed to examine the global mRNA landscape at the transcription level.
source: Illumina RNA-seq datasets from these neurons were analyzed to examine the global mRNA landscape at the transcription level.
evidence: This describes the data analysis approach used in previous studies.

claim: Analysis revealed many cycling transcripts whose abundance changes with time of day that were not identified in previous studies of brain or head tissues.
source: This analysis revealed many cycling transcripts whose abundance changes with time of day that were not identified in previous studies of brain or head tissues (McDonald and Rosbash, 2001; Claridge-Chang et al., 2001; Wijnen et al., 2006; Rodriguez et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and describes findings from prior work.

claim: Many neuron-specific transcripts including novel circadian neuropeptides were revealed.
source: In addition, many neuron-specific transcripts including novel circadian neuropeptides were revealed.
evidence: This describes findings from previous studies on these neurons.

claim: Post-transcriptional level regulation, such as alternative pre-mRNA splicing, is essential for the normal functioning of the nervous system.
source: Besides transcriptional level gene regulation, post-transcriptional level regulation, such as alternative pre-mRNA splicing, is also known to be essential for the normal functioning of the nervous system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of AS in the nervous system.

claim: Alternative pre-mRNA splicing (AS) is a major gene regulatory mechanism that enables a single gene locus to produce populations of often functionally distinct mRNAs in a tissue- or cell-type-specific manner, greatly diversifying the metazoan transcriptome.
source: Alternative pre-mRNA splicing (AS) is a major gene regulatory mechanism that enables a single gene locus to produce populations of often functionally distinct mRNAs in a tissue- or cell-type-specific manner, greatly diversifying the metazoan transcriptome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of AS.

claim: The nervous system is well recognized to exhibit extraordinarily complex and diverse AS patterns in a variety of metazoan organisms.
source: The nervous system is well recognized to exhibit extraordinarily complex and diverse AS patterns in a variety of metazoan organisms (Li et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2008; Irimia et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Diversified AS patterns have been shown to play important roles in modulating numerous neuronal states and activities.
source: Importantly, these diversified AS patterns have been shown to play important roles in modulating numerous neuronal states and activities (Vuong et al., 2016; Norris and Calarco, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Many neuronal receptors such as the NMDA receptors undergo AS that results in functionally distinct proteins that are regulated in different ways to directly affect neuronal membrane depolarization and action-potential firing.
source: For example, many neuronal receptors such as the NMDA receptors undergo AS that results in functionally distinct proteins that are regulated in different ways to directly affect neuronal membrane depolarization and action-potential firing (Chandrasekar, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Recent findings reported several cases where AS is involved in the modulation of the circadian clock in plants, mice and Drosophila.
source: Recent findings reported several cases where AS is involved in the modulation of the circadian clock in plants, mice and Drosophila (Sanchez et al., 2010; Petrillo et al., 2011; McGlincy et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2012; Preußner et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: A comprehensive understanding of AS profiles and their role in circadian clock regulation remains largely unexplored.
source: However, a comprehensive understanding of AS profiles and their role in circadian clock regulation remains largely unexplored.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: It has been difficult to detect cycling of alternatively spliced transcripts because heterogeneous tissues can often mask cell-type specific transcript cycling.
source: As most studies profiling the Drosophila neuronal transcriptome originate from head samples, it has been difficult to detect cycling of alternatively spliced transcripts because heterogeneous tissues can often mask cell-type specific transcript cycling (Kula-Eversole et al., 2010; Nagoshi et al., 2010; Abruzzi et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and explains a methodological challenge.

claim: Currently most AS analysis software for short-read Illumina RNA-seq data depend on pre-annotated libraries of known spliced transcripts, making it difficult to detect and quantitate novel neuronal AS events that prevail in neuronal tissues.
source: In addition, currently most AS analysis software for short-read Illumina RNA-seq data depend on pre-annotated libraries of known spliced transcripts, making it difficult to detect and quantitate novel neuronal AS events that prevail in neuronal tissues.
evidence: This statement describes a limitation of existing computational methods.

claim: JUM is able to identify, quantitate and categorize tissue-specific AS patterns from RNA-seq datasets without the need for or use of prior genome or transcriptome annotations.
source: Here, we have comprehensively analyzed the global AS profiles in the transcriptomes of manually dissected DN1, LNd, and LNv circadian neurons, as well as the non-circadian, TH control neurons described above, using a new computational tool called JUM (the Junction Usage Model) (Wang and Rio, 2017a). JUM is able to identify, quantitate and categorize tissue-specific AS patterns from RNA-seq datasets without the need for or use of prior genome or transcriptome annotations.
evidence: This describes the capability of the JUM method and is supported by a citation.

claim: Using JUM, hundreds of previously unannotated pre-mRNA isoforms were identified.
source: Using JUM, we identify hundreds of previously unannotated pre-mRNA isoforms.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Previously unannotated pre-mRNA isoforms differ extensively among the four neuronal subgroups and were totally missed when RNA-seq data from the heterogeneous fly head sample was analyzed using identical methods.
source: They differ extensively among the four neuronal subgroups and were totally missed when RNA-seq data from the heterogeneous fly head sample was analyzed using identical methods.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing neuron-specific and head RNA-seq data.

claim: Gene ontology analysis of differentially spliced mRNAs in circadian neurons versus non-circadian neurons revealed that they are enriched for transcripts encoding potassium channels, a hallmark of neuronal excitability.
source: Gene ontology analysis of differentially spliced mRNAs in circadian neurons versus non-circadian neurons revealed that they are enriched for transcripts encoding potassium channels, a hallmark of neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis of the study's data.

claim: New alternatively spliced variants and cycling AS patterns were discovered in transcripts encoding proteins of the molecular clock including the photoreceptor Cryptochrome and the kinase Shaggy.
source: In addition, we discovered many new alternatively spliced variants and cycling AS patterns in transcripts encoding proteins of the molecular clock including the photoreceptor Cryptochrome and the kinase Shaggy.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis.

claim: A large set of transcripts exhibit cycling patterns of alternative splicing throughout the day-night cycle, potentially contributing to the normal functioning of the circadian clock.
source: Importantly, we also identified a large set of transcripts that exhibit cycling patterns of alternative splicing throughout the day-night cycle, potentially contributing to the normal functioning of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's time-course analysis.

claim: Post-transcriptional processes like AS impact cell type specification, diversity and function in the brain.
source: This study highlights and reinforces the idea that post-transcriptional processes like AS impact cell type specification, diversity and function in the brain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Total RNA and then mRNA from ~100 manually isolated neurons were purified from entrained flies every four hours across two days (12 samples for each group).
source: Total RNA and then mRNA from ~100 manually isolated neurons were purified from entrained flies every four hours across two days (12 samples for each group).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: A mixture of oligo-dT and random-primed cDNA was used to create RNA-seq libraries from each sample.
source: A mixture of oligo-dT and random-primed cDNA was used to create RNA-seq libraries from each sample, as previously described (Abruzzi et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the library preparation method used in the study.

claim: JUM exclusively utilizes RNA-seq reads that map to splice junctions for AS analysis and defines alternatively spliced junctions (AS junctions) as splice junctions that have alternative 5' - or 3'- splice sites.
source: JUM exclusively utilizes RNA-seq reads that map to splice junctions for AS analysis and defines alternatively spliced junctions (AS junctions) as splice junctions that have alternative 5' - or 3'- splice sites (Figure 1A; left panel).
evidence: This describes the computational method used in the study and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A total of ~6,000 AS junctions were identified in each of the distinct neuronal subtypes that reside in ~2000 genes.
source: We identified a total of ~6,000 AS junctions in each of the distinct neuronal subtypes that reside in ~2000 genes, and ~14,000 AS junctions in heads that reside in ~3000 genes (Figure 1B; Figure 1—source data 1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ~14,000 AS junctions were identified in heads that reside in ~3000 genes.
source: We identified a total of ~6,000 AS junctions in each of the distinct neuronal subtypes that reside in ~2000 genes, and ~14,000 AS junctions in heads that reside in ~3000 genes (Figure 1B; Figure 1—source data 1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Approximately 20% of head AS junctions are novel, that is, they were unannotated in the current Drosophila genome annotation, and these novel AS junctions are found in 1320 genes.
source: Approximately 20% of these head AS junctions are novel, that is, they were unannotated in the current Drosophila genome annotation, and these novel AS junctions are found in 1320 genes (Figure 1B; light blue).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Many AS junctions were identified exclusively in each of the neuronal subpopulations compared to fly heads (~2300 in total, in 839 genes).
source: Importantly, many AS junctions were identified exclusively in each of the neuronal subpopulations compared to fly heads (~2300 in total, in 839 genes; Figure 1B; red), and nearly all of them (~95%) were novel, that is, they had not been previously annotated in the current Drosophila genome annotation (genome version: FB2017_05; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Nearly all (~95%) of the AS junctions identified exclusively in neuronal subpopulations were novel, that is, they had not been previously annotated in the current Drosophila genome annotation.
source: Importantly, many AS junctions were identified exclusively in each of the neuronal subpopulations compared to fly heads (~2300 in total, in 839 genes; Figure 1B; red), and nearly all of them (~95%) were novel, that is, they had not been previously annotated in the current Drosophila genome annotation (genome version: FB2017_05; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Approximately 60% of the novel AS junctions (1398 within 383 genes) are present in all 4 groups of neurons but not present in heads.
source: Indeed, approximately 60% of the novel AS junctions (1398 within 383 genes) are present in all 4 groups of neurons but not present in heads (Figure 1D; bottom left).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Novel AS junctions present in all 4 groups of neurons but not in heads may be common splice junctions of transcripts that are not ubiquitous and therefore less abundant and not detectable in head transcriptomes.
source: These may be common splice junctions of transcripts that are not ubiquitous and therefore less abundant and not detectable in head transcriptomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data regarding why certain junctions are not detected in heads.

claim: The remaining 40% of the novel AS junctions (889) are specific to one or more of the neuron groups and are from 610 genes.
source: The remaining 40% of the novel AS junctions (889) are specific to one or more of the neuron groups (Figure 1D; bottom leftmost) and are from 610 genes.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Novel AS junctions specific to one or more neuron groups may specify cell-type-specific protein isoforms resulting in functional differences between the neurons.
source: These junctions may therefore specify cell-type-specific protein isoforms resulting in functional differences between the neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of neuron-specific AS junctions.

claim: 1,436 AS junctions were identified in fly heads but not in any of the four neuronal groups and are from 812 genes.
source: Another 1,436 AS junctions were identified in fly heads but not in any of the four neuronal groups (Figure 1C,D) and are from 812 genes; these junctions may be non-neuronal, for example, from glia, or they may derive from neurons other than the four groups characterized here.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: AS junctions identified in fly heads but not in any of the four neuronal groups may be non-neuronal, for example, from glia, or they may derive from neurons other than the four groups characterized here.
source: Another 1,436 AS junctions were identified in fly heads but not in any of the four neuronal groups (Figure 1C,D) and are from 812 genes; these junctions may be non-neuronal, for example, from glia, or they may derive from neurons other than the four groups characterized here.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the origin of head-specific AS junctions.

claim: 4,374 AS junctions are identified in fly heads as well as in a subset of the neuronal groups and are from 2084 genes.
source: Finally, 4,374 AS junctions are identified in fly heads as well as in a subset of the neuronal groups and are from 2084 genes (Figure 1D; bottom rightmost).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The identified novel AS junctions are predicted to encode protein isoforms that may impact the function of their specific neuron groups.
source: Importantly, these identified novel AS junctions are predicted to encode protein isoforms that may impact the function of their specific neuron groups.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the potential functional significance of the novel AS junctions.

claim: Gene ontology analysis reveals that the novel AS junctions impact crucial functions in each of these neuron subgroups including neurotransmitter secretion in LNvs, acetylcholine-activated cation-selective channel activity (covering five different subunits of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors) and synaptic target recognition in LNds, potassium ion transporters and locomotor rhythms in DN1s, and chemical synaptic transmission in THs.
source: Gene ontology analysis reveals that the novel AS junctions impact crucial functions in each of these neuron subgroups including neurotransmitter secretion in LNvs, acetylcholine-activated cation-selective channel activity (covering five different subunits of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors) and synaptic target recognition in LNds, potassium ion transporters and locomotor rhythms in DN1s, and chemical synaptic transmission in THs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: cry has a novel splice junction in DN1 and LNd neurons, which is absent in the LNv, TH and head samples.
source: One of the circadian genes that shows a novel AS junction in DN1s is the circadian photoreceptor cryptochrome (cry). cry has a novel splice junction in DN1 and LNd neurons, which is absent in the LNv, TH and head samples (Figure 2A; the sashimi plot indicates the number of sequencing reads spanning the splice junctions [Katz et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The novel AS junction in cry spans from the 5'- splice site right after the first exon to an alternative 3'-splice site in the first intron of cry and results in a truncated, short transcript and presumptive short protein isoform that lacks the functional domains of cry.
source: This novel AS junction spans from the 5'- splice site right after the first exon to an alternative 3'-splice site in the first intron of cry and results in a truncated, short transcript and presumptive short protein isoform that lacks the functional domains of cry.
evidence: This describes the structural consequence of the novel AS junction in cry.

claim: Approximately 20% of the DN1 and approximately 28% of the LNd cry transcripts are spliced into the short transcript isoform.
source: Approximately 20% of the DN1 (Figure 2A) and approximately 28% of the LNd (Figure 2A) cry transcripts are spliced into this short transcript isoform.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CG10483 transcripts encoding a putative G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) experience a novel exon skipping event only in LNds and DN1.
source: Furthermore, CG10483 transcripts encoding a putative G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) experience a novel exon skipping event (Figure 2B; skipped exon marked by '*') only in LNds and DN1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The novel exon skipping event in CG10483 cleanly removes ~65 aa from the receptor transmembrane regions in the middle of the protein.
source: This event cleanly removes ~65 aa from the receptor transmembrane regions in the middle of the protein.
evidence: This describes the structural consequence of the exon skipping event in CG10483.

claim: 249, 194 and 70 AS events are significantly differentially spliced in the DN1, LNv and LNd neurons compared to the TH neurons, respectively, which cover all five conventionally classified AS patterns.
source: Using this method, we found 249, 194 and 70 AS events that are significantly differentially spliced in the DN1, LNv and LNd neurons compared to the TH neurons, respectively, which cover all five conventionally classified AS patterns (Figure 3A; Materials and methods; Figure 3—source data 1–3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the differential AS analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority of the differentially spliced AS events in DN1, LNv or LNd neurons, compared to TH neurons, are unique to each of the circadian neuronal subtypes.
source: Remarkably, the majority of the differentially spliced AS events in DN1, LNv or LNd neurons, compared to TH neurons, are unique to each of the circadian neuronal subtypes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the overlap analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only approximately 1.6–6.6% (9-36) of differentially spliced AS events were found to overlap between 2 of the three circadian neuronal subgroups, which is significantly lower than expected.
source: Only approximately 1.6–6.6% (9-36) of these differentially spliced AS events were found to overlap between 2 of the three circadian neuronal subgroups, which is significantly lower than expected (Hypergeometric Test; p value = 2.38e-07 for DN1/TH and LNd/TH; p value = 3.68e-39 for DN1/TH and LNv/TH; p value = 1.7e-04 for LNd/TH and LNv/TH).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the overlap analysis.

claim: Only 1.8% (8) of differentially spliced AS events are found in all three circadian neuron groups.
source: Only 1.8% (8) of these differentially spliced AS events are found in all three circadian neuron groups.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the overlap analysis.

claim: Three of the eight genes with differentially spliced AS events in all three circadian neuron groups are involved in regulating neuronal plasticity, remodeling and synaptic transmission (Pten, Sap47, Rim).
source: Three of these eight genes are involved in regulating neuronal plasticity, remodeling and synaptic transmission (Pten, Sap47, Rim).
evidence: This describes the functional categories of genes with shared differential AS events.

claim: Each circadian neuronal subgroup possesses a unique pattern of AS isoforms that contribute to the identity of each distinct neuronal group.
source: This result suggests that each circadian neuronal subgroup possesses a unique pattern of AS isoforms that contribute to the identity of each distinct neuronal group (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that most differential AS events are neuron-specific.

claim: Each circadian neuron subpopulation expresses its own unique set of differentially expressed RBPs compared to TH neurons, with very limited overlap.
source: Interestingly, each circadian neuron subpopulation expresses its own unique set of differentially expressed RBPs compared to TH neurons, with very limited overlap (Figure 3B, lower left panel).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Syb and mub, two RBPs that are differentially expressed in LNv neurons compared to TH neurons, target 23 and 32 LNv-specific differentially spliced AS target RNAs in LNv versus TH neurons, respectively, with five overlaps, which covers ~36% of total LNv neuron specific differentially spliced AS events.
source: For example, Syb and mub, two RBPs that are differentially expressed in LNv neurons compared to TH neurons, target 23 and 32 LNv-specific differentially spliced AS target RNAs in LNv versus TH neurons, respectively, with five overlaps, which covers ~36% of total LNv neuron specific differentially spliced AS events.
evidence: This is a finding from integrating differential expression data with CLIP/RIP-seq data.

claim: Circadian neuron-specific RBP expression could drive much of the observed circadian neuron-specific AS patterns compared to TH neurons.
source: Although speculative, this analysis highlights the possibility that circadian neuron-specific RBP expression could drive much of the observed circadian neuron-specific AS patterns compared to TH neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the RBP expression and AS pattern data.

claim: The neuronal synaptobrevin (N-syb) transcript shows a much higher inclusion frequency of an exon present in N-syb variant J in LNv cells (85%) compared to LNd, DN1 and TH neurons (25–36%).
source: One example of a differentially spliced transcript in LNv neurons compared to TH neurons is the neuronal synaptobrevin (N-syb) transcript. It shows a much higher inclusion frequency of an exon (Figure 4A; marked by '*') present in N-syb variant J. 85% of n-Syb transcripts in LNv cells utilize this exon compared to 25–36% in LNd, DN1 and TH neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Inclusion of the alternative exon in N-syb should give rise to a unique protein of 206 amino acids containing an alternative 85 bp C-terminus.
source: Inclusion of this exon should give rise to a unique protein of 206 amino acids containing an alternative 85 bp C-terminus.
evidence: This describes the predicted protein consequence of the AS event in N-syb.

claim: The transcript of the potassium-gated voltage channel, Shab, undergoes differential alternative splicing in LNvs and DN1s.
source: The potassium channel Shab also undergoes alternative 3'-splice site use. In TH and LNd neurons the Shab transcripts preferentially utilize an alternative terminal exon (Figure 4B; marked by '*').
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The alternative terminal exon in Shab results in a significantly shorter isoform and encodes a protein lacking the sixth transmembrane region of the potassium channel protein, which function as a dominant negative protein.
source: It results in a significantly shorter isoform and encodes a protein lacking the sixth transmembrane region of the potassium channel protein (Figure 4B), which function as a dominant negative protein.
evidence: This describes the structural and functional consequence of the AS event in Shab.

claim: 61–74% of Shab transcripts encode the short isoform in TH and LNd neurons, whereas the ratio of the short isoform decreases significantly, to 10 and 40%, in LNvs and DN1s.
source: 61–74% of Shab transcripts encode this short isoform in TH and LNd neurons, whereas with the ratio of the short isoform decreases significantly, to 10 and 40%, in LNvs and DN1s (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Potassium ion transport was the top GO term for both the DN1 and LNv neurons in gene ontology analysis of genes with significantly differentially spliced AS events.
source: Interestingly, potassium ion transport was the top GO term for both the DN1 and LNv neurons (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The differentially spliced AS events include six different potassium channels, as well as two sodium-potassium-exchanging ATPases.
source: The differentially spliced AS events include six different potassium channels, as well as two sodium-potassium-exchanging ATPases (see Shab (above) and Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential AS analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ion channels that undergo differential splicing in circadian neurons modulate neuronal excitability and many of them have been implicated in controlling both circadian locomotor activity and sleep.
source: These ion channels modulate neuronal excitability and many of them have been implicated in controlling both circadian locomotor activity and sleep (Jaramillo et al., 2004; Cirelli et al., 2005; Pimentel et al., 2016; Fogle et al., 2015, see Discussion).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Notable GO terms in the LNv neuronal population are neuronal projection (Fas2, unc-13, Slo, Dscam1, Stai), terminal bouton (cpx, Rab3-GEF, Syn, unc-13 and n-syb) and synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Tomosyn, cpx, syn, unc-13, Rim).
source: Other notable GO terms in the LNv neuronal population are neuronal projection (Fas2, unc-13, Slo, Dscam1, Stai), terminal bouton (cpx, Rab3-GEF, Syn, unc-13 and n-syb) and synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Tomosyn, cpx, syn, unc-13, Rim).
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis of LNv differential AS events.

claim: LNv neurons exhibit highly dynamic neuronal projections that undergo time-of-day dependent morphological changes and synaptic vesicle localization.
source: These GO terms capture some of the unique features of the LNv neuronal population: they exhibit highly dynamic neuronal projections that undergo time-of-day dependent morphological changes and synaptic vesicle localization (Fernández et al., 2008; Gorostiza et al., 2014; Petsakou et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Notable GO terms for the DN1s include the calcium-calmodulin-dependent family of protein kinases (CASK, CAMKI, CAMKII, and CG17528), as well as sodium ion transporters (Nhe3, Nckx30c, NaCP60E, Atpalpha, nrv3).
source: Other notable GO terms for the DN1s include the calcium-calmodulin-dependent family of protein kinases (CASK, CAMKI, CAMKII, and CG17528), as well as sodium ion transporters (Nhe3, Nckx30c, NaCP60E, Atpalpha, nrv3).
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis of DN1 differential AS events.

claim: The alternatively spliced cassette exons are somewhat more conserved than the non-alternatively spliced cassette exons, although the result is not statistically significant.
source: Interestingly, the alternatively spliced cassette exons are somewhat more conserved than the non-alternatively spliced cassette exons, although the result is not statistically significant (Mann-Whitney U Test; p value 0.17).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-species conservation analysis.

claim: The inclusion/exclusion of the alternatively spliced cassette exons are more prone to preserve reading frame than non-alternatively spliced exons.
source: We also found that the inclusion/exclusion of the alternatively spliced cassette exons are more prone to preserve reading frame than non-alternatively spliced exons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), further indicating that these AS events are important to the identity and function of the neuron subpopulation.
evidence: This is a finding from reading frame preservation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: 173 AS structures cycle in DN1 neurons (5.7% of all AS structures), 92 in LNv neurons (5.0% of all AS structures), and 48 in LNd neurons (3.7% of all AS structures).
source: We identified cycling AS structures in all 3 groups of circadian neurons: 173 AS structures in DN1 neurons (5.7% of all AS structures), 92 in LNv neurons (5.0% of all AS structures), and 48 in LNd neurons (3.7% of all AS structures) (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the cycling AS analysis.

claim: Cycling AS structures affect 147, 81, 43, and nine genes in DN1, LNv, LNd and TH neurons, respectively.
source: These events affect 147, 81, 43, and nine genes in DN1, LNv, LNd and TH neurons, respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the cycling AS analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 85% of the transcripts that exhibit time-dependent changes in alternative splicing do not cycle at the total mRNA level.
source: Importantly, 85% of the transcripts that exhibit time-dependent changes in alternative splicing do not cycle at the total mRNA level (Figure 6A; RPKM based on ESAT quantification [Derr et al., 2016; Abruzzi et al., 2017]).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing cycling AS with cycling mRNA levels shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Most cycling AS structures are neuron specific; only two transcripts undergo cycling AS in all three groups of circadian neurons.
source: The majority of these cycling AS structures are specific to a particular group of circadian neurons (Figure 6B). Some of this specificity is because certain AS structures are only found in one subgroup of circadian neurons (~40% in DN1, 14% in LNd and 25% in LNv). Moreover, only two transcripts show cycling alternative splicing in all three groups of circadian neurons: still life (sif) that regulates synaptic differentiation and the type II Camp-dependent protein kinase, pKa-R1 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the overlap analysis of cycling AS shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Time-of-day changes in alternative pre-mRNA splicing acts as an additional and previously unappreciated level of circadian regulation in Drosophila clock neurons.
source: This striking specificity suggests that time-of-day changes in alternative pre-mRNA splicing acts as an additional and previously unappreciated level of circadian regulation in Drosophila clock neurons, as previously suggested in mammals based on microarrays (McGlincy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cycling AS findings, supported by a citation to previous work in mammals.

claim: Alternative splicing of the sgg transcript is due to the use of two different 3'- splice sites generating distinct transcript and protein isoforms differing at the C terminus: a shorter isoform utilizing terminal Exon b and a longer isoform utilizing terminal Exon a that includes a specific additional 63 amino acids.
source: One striking example of a cycling AS structure is a transcript isoform encoding circadian kinase, Shaggy (from the fly gene sgg; known in mammals as GSK3). Alternative splicing of the sgg transcript is due to the use of two different 3'- splice sites generating distinct transcript and protein isoforms differing at the C terminus: a shorter isoform utilizing terminal Exon b and a longer isoform utilizing terminal Exon a that includes a specific additional 63 amino acids (Figure 6C; marked by '*' and '**', respectively).
evidence: This describes the AS event in sgg shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In LNv and DN1 neurons, the longer sgg isoform is almost exclusively used.
source: In LNv and DN1 neurons, the longer sgg isoform is almost exclusively used (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In LNd neurons, the longer sgg isoform is utilized almost exclusively in the morning (ZT0-ZT11) and then by late night (ZT18-24) there is approximately equal usage of the long and short sgg transcripts.
source: However, in LNd neurons, the longer isoform is utilized almost exclusively in the morning (ZT0-ZT11) and then by late night (ZT18-24) there is approximately equal usage of the long and short sgg transcripts (Figure 6C; two replicates quantified in Figure 6D, red line and circle).
evidence: This is a finding from the time-course analysis shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: The potassium channel SLOWPOKE is encoded by the Slo gene and undergoes neuron-specific AS cycling.
source: The potassium channel SLOWPOKE is encoded by the Slo gene and also undergoes neuron-specific AS cycling.
evidence: This is a finding from the cycling AS analysis.

claim: There are two mutually exclusively used exons in the second alternatively spliced exonic regions in the Slo transcript: exon 2a and exon 2b that alter the cytosolic face of the channel.
source: There are two mutually exclusively used exons in the second alternatively spliced exonic regions in the Slo transcript: exon 2a and exon 2b that alter the cytosolic face of the channel (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, marked by '*' and '**', respectively).
evidence: This describes the AS event in Slo shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In DN1 neurons only, exon 2b of Slo is included in the mornings and then there is a shift toward exon 2a inclusion in the late nighttime.
source: In DN1 neurons only, exon 2b is included in the mornings and then there is a shift toward exon 2a inclusion in the late nighttime (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the time-course analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: SLOWPOKE has been shown to affect circadian behavior in Drosophila.
source: SLOWPOKE has been shown to affect circadian behavior in Drosophila (Ceriani et al., 2002), and its mammalian homolog, Kcnma1, shows similar phenotypes in mammals (Meredith et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The mammalian homolog of SLOWPOKE, Kcnma1, shows similar phenotypes in mammals.
source: SLOWPOKE has been shown to affect circadian behavior in Drosophila (Ceriani et al., 2002), and its mammalian homolog, Kcnma1, shows similar phenotypes in mammals (Meredith et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The different protein isoforms created by time-of-day changes in alternative splicing mRNA isoforms are possibly important for circadian functions.
source: It is possible that the different protein isoforms created by time-of-day changes in alternative splicing mRNA isoforms are important for these functions (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of cycling AS.

claim: Modulation of locomotor behavior is enriched for cycling AS transcripts in all three circadian neuron groups, although a distinct group of transcripts is implicated in each circadian neuronal group.
source: Interestingly, modulation of locomotor behavior is enriched for cycling AS transcripts in all three circadian neuron groups, although a distinct group of transcripts is implicated in each circadian neuronal group (Figure 6—figure supplement 3; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: In LNvs and LNds neurons, the most significantly enriched GO term for cycling AS transcripts is male courtship behavior and olfactory learning, respectively.
source: In LNvs and LNds neurons, the most significantly enriched GO term for cycling AS transcripts is male courtship behavior and olfactory learning, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: In DN1 neurons, the top enriched GO term for cycling AS transcripts is mRNA binding proteins and 8 out of the 12 genes in this category encode alternative splicing regulators.
source: In DN1 neurons, the top enriched GO term for cycling AS transcripts is mRNA binding proteins and 8 out of the 12 genes in this category encode alternative splicing regulators.
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis.

claim: The cycling AS of splicing regulators could further facilitate downstream time of day-dependent changes in global splicing profiles.
source: The cycling AS of these splicing regulators could further facilitate downstream time of day-dependent changes in global splicing profiles (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the potential regulatory role of cycling AS in splicing regulators.

claim: mRNAs cycle with distinct phases in each subgroup of neurons.
source: Previous analysis of mRNA expression cycling in the circadian neurons revealed that mRNAs cycle with distinct phases in each subgroup of neurons (Abruzzi et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The phases of the cycling AS structures show neuron-group specific distributions.
source: Interestingly, the phases of the cycling AS structures also show neuron-group specific distributions (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the phase analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In DN1 neurons, the majority of the time-of-day-dependent cycling AS structures peak in the late night, which is almost anti-phase to that of DN1 mRNA cycling.
source: Most interesting were the DN1 neurons in which the majority of the time-of-day-dependent cycling AS structures peak in the late night (Figure 7A; blue). This peak is almost anti-phase to that of DN1 mRNA cycling (Figure 7A, red).
evidence: This is a finding from the phase analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In LNv neurons, mRNA cycling and AS cycling show similar phases.
source: In contrast, mRNA cycling and AS cycling show similar phases in the LNv neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the phase analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In LNd neurons, cycling mRNAs peak in the early evening, but cycling AS structures have a random distribution throughout the day.
source: The LNd neurons have a third pattern: cycling mRNAs peak in the early evening, but cycling AS structures have a random distribution throughout the day (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the phase analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Every circadian neuron expresses a unique set of cycling RBPs.
source: To probe potential mechanisms contributing to this neuron-specific AS cycling, we queried the list of cycling mRNAs within these neurons (Abruzzi et al., 2017) and identified cycling transcripts encoding RBPs in all three neuronal subgroups (Figure 7B). None of the identified RBP mRNAs cycle in more than one circadian neuron subgroup.
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing cycling RBP expression shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Qkr54B, a cycling splicing factor in LNds, has been shown to target Sgg transcripts.
source: Although there was no clear global correlation between the phases of these RBP mRNAs and cycling AS in any neuronal group, we did identify a cycling splicing factor in LNds, Qkr54B, that has been shown to target Sgg transcripts (Stoiber et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Qkr54B mRNA peaks 3–4 hr prior to the time of day dependent inclusion of the alternative spliced Sgg terminal Exon b.
source: Interestingly, Qkr54B mRNA peaks 3–4 hr prior to the time of day dependent inclusion of the alternative spliced Sgg terminal Exon b (Figure 6D; green line and triangle), suggesting that cycling RBP expression might contribute to the cycling AS patterns.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-course analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cycling RBP expression might contribute to the cycling AS patterns.
source: Interestingly, Qkr54B mRNA peaks 3–4 hr prior to the time of day dependent inclusion of the alternative spliced Sgg terminal Exon b (Figure 6D; green line and triangle), suggesting that cycling RBP expression might contribute to the cycling AS patterns.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal relationship between Qkr54B expression and Sgg AS.

claim: Tissues of the nervous and germline systems, such as brain, testes and ovaries, have more complex transcriptomes than other cell types due to extensive alternative pre-mRNA splicing or AS.
source: Tissues of the nervous and germline systems, such as brain, testes and ovaries, have more complex transcriptomes than other cell types due to extensive alternative pre-mRNA splicing or AS (Wang et al., 2008; Pan et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The nervous system exhibits vast numbers of AS isoforms, many of which are novel and are only beginning to be comprehensively identified.
source: The nervous system especially exhibits vast numbers of AS isoforms, many of which are novel and are only beginning to be comprehensively identified (Li et al., 2007; Irimia et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The increase in transcript isoform complexity likely contributes to the specification and functional diversity of cell types within the nervous system.
source: This increase in transcript isoform complexity likely contributes to the specification and functional diversity of cell types within the nervous system.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established knowledge about AS in the nervous system.

claim: Many of the novel, previously undetected and unannotated isoforms were unique to a given neuronal population and occurred in transcripts from genes implicated in neuronal activity or circadian rhythms.
source: This is because many of these novel, previously undetected and unannotated isoforms were unique to a given neuronal population and occurred in transcripts from genes implicated in neuronal activity or circadian rhythms.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings regarding the specificity and functional relevance of novel AS isoforms.

claim: The kinase Shaggy and the blue light photoreceptor cryptochrome play central roles in circadian clock regulation and have novel AS patterns in discrete subsets of the circadian neurons.
source: For example, the kinase Shaggy and the blue light photoreceptor cryptochrome play central roles in circadian clock regulation and have novel AS patterns in discrete subsets of the circadian neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of specific findings from the study.

claim: Nine different transcripts involved in potassium transport undergo differential AS in circadian neurons compared to non-circadian neurons.
source: In addition, nine different transcripts involved in potassium transport undergo differential AS in circadian neurons compared to non-circadian neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the differential AS analysis.

claim: Many potassium channel genes have a complex organization known to encode populations of functionally distinct proteins isoforms, which change the activation kinetics as well as calcium sensitivity of the channels.
source: Many of these genes have a complex organization known to encode populations of functionally distinct proteins isoforms, which change the activation kinetics as well as calcium sensitivity of the channels (Johnson et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neuronal firing is known to play a key role in the circadian circuit with recent studies illustrating that different subgroups of circadian neurons have characteristic time-of-day neuronal firing patterns.
source: Neuronal firing is known to play a key role in the circadian circuit with recent studies illustrating that different subgroups of circadian neurons have characteristic time-of-day neuronal firing patterns (Flourakis et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Several channel pre-mRNAs that undergo differential splicing in circadian neurons impact circadian behavior and sleep, such as slowpoke (Slo), Shaker (Sh), and Hyperkinetic (Hk).
source: Although it is not yet fully understood which potassium channels play a critical role in each circadian neuron subgroup, several channel pre-mRNAs that undergo differential splicing in circadian neurons impact circadian behavior and sleep, such as slowpoke (Slo [Jaramillo et al., 2004]), Shaker (Sh; [Cirelli et al., 2005; Pimentel et al., 2016]) and Hyperkinetic (Hk; [Fogle et al., 2015]).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AS likely adds diversity and distinct physiological properties to potassium channel protein isoforms, which then impacts neuron-specific firing patterns.
source: It is therefore likely that AS adds diversity and distinct physiological properties to these protein isoforms, which then impacts neuron-specific firing patterns.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the potential functional significance of AS in potassium channels.

claim: AS augments transcriptional regulation in giving different circadian neurons individual identities and distinct functions.
source: From a more general perspective, AS augments transcriptional regulation in giving different circadian neurons individual identities and distinct functions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall role of AS in circadian neuron diversity.

claim: Approximately 5% of the AS events identified in circadian neurons undergo time-of-day dependent changes in alternative splicing (cycling splicing).
source: Approximately 5% of the AS events identified in circadian neurons also undergo time-of-day dependent changes in alternative splicing (cycling splicing).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the cycling AS findings.

claim: All experiments were conducted under 12 hr of light and 12 hr of dark conditions, making it impossible to distinguish between light and clock control.
source: It is important to note that all our experiments were conducted under 12 hr of light and 12 hr of dark conditions, making it impossible to distinguish between light and clock control.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: Splicing adds a dramatic layer of gene regulation to diurnal changes in gene expression.
source: Nonetheless, these data indicate that splicing adds a dramatic layer of gene regulation to diurnal changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cycling AS findings.

claim: Many of the cycling AS transcripts show constant overall mRNA levels, which suggests the existence of neuron-specific splicing factors that are expressed or activated only at specific times of the day.
source: Moreover, many of the cycling AS transcripts show constant overall mRNA levels, which suggests the existence of neuron-specific splicing factors that are expressed or activated only at specific times of the day.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that many cycling AS transcripts do not show cycling mRNA levels.

claim: Several candidate cycling neuron-enriched transcripts that encode RBPs may help to drive cycling AS patterns have been identified.
source: Indeed, we have identified several candidate cycling neuron-enriched transcripts that encode RBPs that may help to drive cycling AS patterns.
evidence: This is a summary of findings regarding cycling RBPs.

claim: One recent study was able to obtain about 20M sequence reads per isolated human iPS cell but only managed to analyze splicing patterns for the most highly expressed genes.
source: One recent study was able to obtain about 20M sequence reads per isolated human iPS cell but only managed to analyze splicing patterns for the most highly expressed genes (Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The study used ~100 isolated Drosophila neurons for each of the four neuron subtypes along with judicious use of both oligo-dT and random hexamer priming of the cDNA libraries.
source: Our study in contrast used ~100 isolated Drosophila neurons for each of the four neuron subtypes along with judicious use of both oligo-dT and random hexamer priming of the cDNA libraries.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The study obtained about 10–30M sequence reads for each sample, including substantial information from the 5' ends of transcripts.
source: This strategy obtained about 10–30M sequence reads for each sample, including substantial information from the 5' ends of transcripts, and JUM was able to detect and classify a large number of previously unannotated pre-mRNA isoforms.
evidence: This describes the sequencing depth achieved in the study.

claim: JUM was able to detect and classify a large number of previously unannotated pre-mRNA isoforms.
source: This strategy obtained about 10–30M sequence reads for each sample, including substantial information from the 5' ends of transcripts, and JUM was able to detect and classify a large number of previously unannotated pre-mRNA isoforms.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings using JUM.

claim: Many novel isoforms are missing from fly head RNA-seq data assayed and analyzed in parallel, indicating that these new isoforms are cell-type specific.
source: Many of them are missing from our fly head RNA-seq data assayed and analyzed in parallel, indicating that these new isoforms are cell-type specific.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing neuron-specific and head RNA-seq data.

claim: The novel isoforms from the three circadian neuron groups fall into many gene ontology (GO) categories associated with specific circadian clock activity and function.
source: Not surprisingly, the novel isoforms from the three circadian neuron groups fall into many gene ontology (GO) categories associated with specific circadian clock activity and function.
evidence: This is a summary of the gene ontology analysis findings.

claim: The number of alternative splicing events that take place in neuronal tissues is grossly underestimated.
source: Taken together, the work presented here indicates that the number of alternative splicing events that take place in neuronal tissues is grossly underestimated, even though publically-funded genome projects, such as the NIH modENCODE projects deeply sequenced transcriptomes from a variety of Drosophila tissues and developmental stages.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of existing genome annotation efforts.

claim: Comprehensive analysis of splicing patterns through deep sequencing of ~50 mouse and human tissues revealed about 2500 neuronally-regulated alternative splicing events.
source: This is despite the appreciation of how much AS occurs in the nervous system, for example recent comprehensive analysis of splicing patterns through deep sequencing of ~50 mouse and human tissues revealed about 2500 neuronally-regulated alternative splicing events (Irimia et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AS events will need to be comprehensively evaluated by much deeper sequencing than is currently afforded by most contemporary single cell RNA-seq studies and by AS analysis software like JUM that is not constrained by a priori knowledge of known splicing events.
source: We therefore suggest that these events will need to be comprehensively evaluated by much deeper sequencing than is currently afforded by most contemporary single cell RNA-seq studies and by AS analysis software like JUM that is not constrained by a priori knowledge of known splicing events.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings and methodological approach.

claim: Almost all AS junctions contain canonical splice sites.
source: Importantly, almost all AS junctions contain canonical splice sites (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the splice site sequences of identified AS junctions.
